claim: Plants create CO2 gradients in the soil with concentrations of 548–554 ppm in the rhizosphere, 506–515 ppm at distances between 8 and 16 cm from the plant, and 460–484 ppm at distances between 16 and 32 cm.
source: We observed a significant CO2 gradient in the soil, with concentrations of 548–554 ppm in the rhizosphere, 506–515 ppm at distances between 8 and 16 cm from the plant, and 460–484 ppm at distances between 16 and 32 cm (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of CO2 levels at different distances from maize seedlings, with data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At distances of more than 40 cm from the plant, CO2 levels levelled off at 425–439 ppm.
source: At distances of more than 40 cm, CO2 levels levelled off at 425–439 ppm.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of CO2 levels at different distances from maize seedlings.

claim: In the absence of plants, no CO2 gradient was observed, and CO2 concentrations in the soil were around 430 ppm.
source: In the absence of the plants, no CO2 gradient was observed, and CO2 concentrations in the soil were around 430 ppm (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of CO2 levels after removing plants from the system, with data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The release of CO2 from maize roots can account for the CO2 difference between soil trays with and without plants.
source: When surrounding soil was removed and seedling roots were washed, we observed 542 ± 6.74 ppm CO2 around the roots (n = 3). Thus, the release of CO2 from maize roots can account for the CO2 difference between soil trays with and without plants.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of CO2 around washed roots and inference from the comparison of CO2 levels with and without plants.

claim: The WCR genome encodes three putative CO2 receptors: DvvGr1, DvvGr2, and DvvGr3.
source: Three putative carbon dioxide receptor candidates, DvvGr1, DvvGr2, and DvvGr3, were identified, matching three candidate genes that were found in previous transcriptome analyses (Rodrigues et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by gene sequence similarity analyses against the WCR genome and previous transcriptomic studies.

claim: DvvGr1 and DvvGr2 expression levels are significantly higher in the head than in the rest of the body of second instar WCR larvae.
source: Expression levels of DvvGr1 and DvvGr2 were found to be significantly higher in the head than in the rest of the body (thorax and abdomen) of second instar WCR larvae (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression measurements comparing head and body tissues, with data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: No significant difference in expression was observed for DvvGr3 between head and body tissues.
source: No significant difference in expression was observed for DvvGr3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression measurements comparing head and body tissues, with data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All three genes encode for 7-transmembrane domain proteins, which is consistent with their roles as receptors.
source: Protein tertiary structure and topology models indicated that all three genes encode for 7-transmembrane domain proteins, which is consistent with their roles as receptors (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by protein structure prediction models shown in Figure 2B-D and established knowledge about receptor protein topology.

claim: Oral administration of dsRNA targeting DvvGr1, DvvGr2, or DvvGr3 reduced the expression levels of these genes by 80%, 83%, and 66% respectively compared to wild type larvae.
source: Oral administration of dsRNA targeting either DvvGr1, DvvGr2, or DvvGr3 reduced the expression levels of these genes by 80%, 83%, and 66% compared to WCR larvae fed with dsRNA of the green fluorescent protein (GFP) gene (herein referred to as wild type [WT]) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression measurements after RNAi treatment, with data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CO2 levels were approximately 100 ppm higher in the arms of the L-shaped pots that contained plastic cups filled with carbonated water than in the arms of L-shaped pots that contained plastic cups filled with distilled water.
source: Measurements within the olfactometers showed that CO2 levels were approximately 100 ppm higher in the arms of the L-shaped pots that contained plastic cups filled with carbonated water than in the arms of L-shaped pots that contained plastic cups filled with distilled water (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CO2 measurements in olfactometers, with data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A higher proportion of wild type larvae moved towards olfactometer arms with higher CO2 levels.
source: A higher proportion of WT larvae moved towards olfactometer arms with higher CO2 levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in olfactometers, with data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Silencing DvvGr1 or DvvGr3 expression did not alter the preference for higher CO2 levels.
source: Silencing DvvGr1 or DvvGr3 expression did not alter this preference.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments comparing wild type and gene-silenced larvae in olfactometers.

claim: DvvGr2-silenced larvae did not show preference for any olfactometer arm.
source: In contrast, DvvGr2-silenced larvae did not show preference for any olfactometer arm (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in olfactometers, with data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DvvGr2-silenced larvae responded similarly to the repellent volatile methyl anthranilate as wild type larvae.
source: DvvGr2-silenced larvae responded similarly to the repellent volatile methyl anthranilate as WT larvae (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments testing responses to methyl anthranilate, with data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Responsiveness to non-volatile compounds such as Fe(III)(DIMBOA)3 and a blend of glucose, fructose, and sucrose was unaltered in DvvGr2-silenced larvae.
source: Responsiveness to non-volatile compounds such as Fe(III)(DIMBOA)3 and a blend of glucose, fructose, and sucrose was also unaltered in DvvGr2-silenced larvae (Figure 3F, G), demonstrating that knocking down DvvGr2 expression does not alter the capacity of WCR larvae to respond to other important chemical cues.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments testing responses to non-volatile compounds, with data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Wild type larvae showed characteristic dose-dependent behavioural responses to CO2, being attracted to CO2 concentrations between 59 and 258 ppm above ambient and repelled by CO2-enriched air at 950 ppm above ambient CO2 levels and above.
source: WT larvae showed characteristic dose-dependent behavioural responses to CO2. While they did not respond to 22 ppm CO2 above ambient CO2 levels, they were attracted to CO2 concentrations between 59 and 258 ppm above ambient and repelled by CO2-enriched air at 950 ppm above ambient CO2 levels and above (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments testing responses to different CO2 concentrations, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DvvGr2-silenced larvae did not respond to CO2 enrichment at any of the tested concentrations.
source: In contrast, DvvGr2-silenced larvae did not respond to CO2 enrichment at any of the tested concentrations (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments testing responses to different CO2 concentrations, with data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DvvGr2 silencing fully and specifically suppresses CO2 responsiveness in WCR larvae.
source: These experiments show that WCR larvae are attracted to CO2-enriched environments within the physiological range of the maize rhizosphere and that DvvGr2 silencing fully and specifically suppresses CO2 responsiveness in WCR larvae.
evidence: Supported by multiple behavioral experiments showing loss of CO2 response but retention of other sensory responses in DvvGr2-silenced larvae.

claim: Wild type larvae made frequent turns, but consistently oriented themselves towards the CO2 release point and stopped moving once they reached it.
source: WT larvae made frequent turns, but consistently oriented themselves towards the CO2 release point. Once they reached the CO2 release point, they stopped moving (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by trajectory tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DvvGr2-silenced larvae exhibited similar turning behaviour as wild type larvae, but did not move towards the CO2 release point.
source: DvvGr2-silenced larvae exhibited similar turning behaviour as WT larvae, but did not move towards the CO2 release point (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by trajectory tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Wild type larvae spend more time on CO2 release point than DvvGr2-silenced larvae.
source: WT larvae spend more time on CO2 release point than DvvGr2-silenced larvae (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: During the movement phase, the mean speed of wild type larvae and DvvGr2-silenced larvae was similar.
source: During the movement phase, the mean speed of WT larvae and DvvGr2-silenced larvae was similar (Figure 5C), but the distance covered by DvvGr2-silenced larvae was higher, as they did not stop at the CO2 release point.
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking experiments, with data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Speed and distance covered were similar between wild type and DvvGr2-silenced larvae in Petri plates with maize roots.
source: Speed and distance covered were similar between WT and DvvGr2-silenced larvae (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by trajectory tracking experiments with maize roots, with data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Both wild type and DvvGr2-silenced larvae oriented themselves towards the maize roots and reached the maize roots after a similar amount of time.
source: Surprisingly, both WT and DvvGr2-silenced larvae oriented themselves towards the maize roots and reached the maize roots after a similar amount of time (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by trajectory tracking experiments with maize roots, with data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: DvvGr2 expression is required for the location and detection of CO2, but does not influence WCR motility nor its ability to locate maize roots over short distances (<9 cm).
source: This result shows that DvvGr2 expression is required for the location and detection of CO2, but does not influence WCR motility nor its ability to locate maize roots over short distances (i.e.,<9 cm).
evidence: Inferred from the combination of behavioral experiments showing similar motility and short-range host location but impaired CO2 detection in DvvGr2-silenced larvae.

claim: The presence of a host root system increased CO2 concentrations by approximately 100 ppm above ambient CO2 levels in the corresponding olfactometer arm.
source: CO2 measurements revealed that the presence of a host root system increased CO2 concentrations by approximately 100 ppm above ambient CO2 levels in the corresponding olfactometer arm (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CO2 measurements in olfactometers with and without plants, with data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Soda lime reduced ambient CO2 concentrations in the olfactometer arms by approximately 100 ppm and equalized CO2 concentrations between arms with and without a host plant.
source: The soda lime reduced ambient CO2 concentrations in the olfactometer arms by approximately 100 ppm and equalized CO2 concentrations between arms with and without a host plant (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by CO2 measurements in olfactometers with soda lime, with data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The diffusion of other maize root volatiles was not affected by the soda lime.
source: The diffusion of other maize root volatiles was not affected by the soda lime (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), thus validating the CO2 scrubbing approach.
evidence: Supported by volatile measurements comparing control and soda lime conditions, with data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: When released at distance of 9 cm from the volatile sources, both wild type and DvvGr2-silenced larvae showed a clear preference for the olfactometer arms leading to host plants.
source: When released at distance of 9 cm from the volatile sources, both WT and DvvGr2-silenced larvae showed a clear preference for the olfactometer arms leading to host plants (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in short-arm olfactometers, with data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The preference for host plants at 9 cm distance was still intact in olfactometers outfitted with soda lime, showing that volatiles other than CO2 are sufficient for volatile-mediated host location at a short distance.
source: This preference was still intact in olfactometers outfitted with soda lime, showing that volatiles other than CO2 are sufficient for volatile-mediated host location at a short distance.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in short-arm olfactometers with soda lime, demonstrating that host location occurs even without CO2 gradients at short distances.

claim: At a distance of 18 cm from the volatile sources, wild type larvae showed a strong preference for arms leading to host plants.
source: At a distance of 18 cm from the volatile sources, WT larvae showed a similarly strong preference for arms leading to host plants (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in long-arm olfactometers, with data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At a distance of 18 cm from the volatile sources, DvvGr2-silenced larvae did not exhibit any preference.
source: By contrast, DvvGr2-silenced larvae did not exhibit any preference (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in long-arm olfactometers, with data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the presence of soda lime at 18 cm distance, neither wild type nor DvvGr2-silenced larvae were attracted to arms with a host plant.
source: In the presence of soda lime, neither WT nor DvvGr2-silenced larvae were attracted to arms with a host plant (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in long-arm olfactometers with soda lime, with data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: WCR larvae use plant-associated CO2 to locate host plants over distances greater than 9 cm in a DvvGr2-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these experiments provide strong support for the hypothesis that WCR larvae use plant-associated CO2 to locate host plants over distances greater than 9 cm in a DvvGr2-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of behavioral experiments showing distance-dependent effects of DvvGr2 silencing and CO2 removal on host location.

claim: The CO2 emitted by maize roots formed a gradient in the soil, starting at about 506 ppm in the rhizosphere (zone 1) and 430 ppm at distances of 16–32 cm from the plant (zone 2).
source: The CO2 emitted by maize roots formed a gradient in the soil, starting at about 506 ppm in the rhizosphere (zone 1) and 430 ppm at distances of 16–32 cm from the plant (zone 2) (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CO2 measurements in soil-filled trays at different distances from plants, with data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: At distances of more than 32 cm from the plant, the CO2 levels were around 400 ppm and statistically indistinguishable from soil without plants or ambient air.
source: At distances of more than 32 cm from the plant, the CO2 levels were around 400 ppm and statistically indistinguishable from soil without plants or ambient air (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CO2 measurements in soil-filled trays at different distances from plants, with data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wild type and DvvGr2-silenced larvae dispersed equally across arenas without host plants, without any difference between the two larval types.
source: We found that the larvae dispersed equally across the arenas, without any difference between WT and DvvGr2-silenced larvae (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in soil arenas without plants, with data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Eight hours after releasing the larvae at 64 cm from the plant, 53% of wild type larvae were retrieved close to the maize rhizosphere (zone 1), while only 33% of the DvvGr2-silenced larvae were recovered from the maize rhizosphere.
source: Eight hours after releasing the larvae into arenas that included host plants on one side, 53% of WT larvae that were released at 64 cm from the plant were retrieved close to the maize rhizosphere, that is, in zone 1 (Figure 7C). In contrast, only 33% of the DvvGr2-silenced larvae that were released at the same distance were recovered from the maize rhizosphere (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in soil arenas with plants, with data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Significantly more DvvGr2-silenced larvae were recovered further away from the plants, in zones 3 and 4.
source: Significantly more DvvGr2-silenced larvae were recovered further away from the plants, in zones 3 and 4 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in soil arenas with plants, with data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The number of wild type and DvvGr2-silenced WCR larvae found close to the host plant increased with decreasing release distance, as did the difference between wild type and DvvGr2-silenced larvae.
source: The number of WT and DvvGr2-silenced WCR larvae found close to the host plant increased with decreasing release distance, as did the difference between WT and DvvGr2-silenced larvae (Figure 7C–F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in soil arenas at different release distances, with data shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: At a release distance of 16 cm, only slightly more wild type than DvvGr2-silenced larvae were found close to the plant roots.
source: At a release distance of 16 cm, only slightly more WT than DvvGr2-silenced larvae were found close to the plant roots (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in soil arenas at 16 cm release distance, with data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Within 10 hr, 36% of the released wild type larvae were found in zone 1, and within 32 hr, this number had increased to 90%.
source: Within 10 hr, 36% of the released WT larvae were found in zone 1, and within 32 hr, this number had increased to 90% (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by time-course behavioral experiments in soil arenas, with data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only 24% of the released DvvGr2-silenced larvae were found in zone 1 after 10 hr, and after 32 hr, this value had only increased to 56%.
source: By contrast, only 24% of the released DvvGr2-silenced larvae were found in zone 1 after 10 hr, and after 32 hr, this value had only increased to 56% (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by time-course behavioral experiments in soil arenas, with data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The capacity to detect CO2 gradients contributes to successful host location by WCR larvae in a distance-specific manner in the soil.
source: Thus, the capacity to detect CO2 gradients contributes to successful host location by WCR larvae in a distance-specific manner in the soil.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of behavioral experiments showing distance-dependent effects of DvvGr2 silencing on host location in soil arenas.

claim: Larvae released at a distance equal to or below 32 cm from the host plant (zones 2–3) can use CO2 directly as a host location cue.
source: While larvae released at a distance equal to or below 32 cm from the host plant (zones 2–3) can use CO2 directly as a host location cue, larvae released at greater distances likely move randomly before reaching zones with plant-associated CO2 gradients.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of CO2 gradient measurements and behavioral experiments at different distances.

claim: Larvae released at greater distances than 32 cm likely move randomly before reaching zones with plant-associated CO2 gradients.
source: While larvae released at a distance equal to or below 32 cm from the host plant (zones 2–3) can use CO2 directly as a host location cue, larvae released at greater distances likely move randomly before reaching zones with plant-associated CO2 gradients.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of CO2 gradient measurements and behavioral experiments at different distances.

claim: Higher CO2 levels were observed close to the roots of plants that were well fertilized compared to the levels that were observed close to the roots of plants that received medium or low fertilizer doses.
source: Higher CO2 levels were observed close to the roots of plants that were well fertilized compared to the levels that were observed close to the roots of plants that received medium (50% of optimally fertilized plants) or low (10% of optimally fertilized plants) fertilizer doses (Figure 8A, B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by CO2 measurements near roots of differentially fertilized plants, with data shown in Figure 8A, B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Soil CO2 levels decreased with increasing distance from the plants and were lowest in the middle of the experimental trays.
source: As observed before, soil CO2 levels decreased with increasing distance from the plants and were lowest in the middle of the experimental trays (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: Supported by CO2 measurements at different distances from plants in experimental trays, with data shown in Figure 8A, B.

claim: Wild type larvae showed a significant preference for well-fertilized over medium- or low-fertilized plants.
source: In choice experiments with maize plants planted approximately 50 cm apart, which corresponds to row spacing used for high planting densities in maize cultivation, WT larvae showed a significant preference for well-fertilized over medium- or low-fertilized plants (Figure 8C, D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral choice experiments with differentially fertilized plants, with data shown in Figure 8C, D.

claim: DvvGr2-silenced larvae did not show any preference between differentially fertilized plants.
source: DvvGr2-silenced larvae did not show any preference (Figure 8C, D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral choice experiments with differentially fertilized plants, with data shown in Figure 8C, D.

claim: WCR larvae gained most weight on washed roots of well-fertilized maize plants than on washed roots of plants treated with medium or low doses of fertilizer.
source: In no-choice experiments, WCR larvae gained most weight on washed roots of well-fertilized maize plants than on washed roots of plants treated with medium or low doses of fertilizer (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by larval performance experiments on differentially fertilized plants, with data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Intact CO2 perception allows WCR larvae to locate suitable host plants at agriculturally relevant distances, which may result in specific insect distribution patterns in heterogeneous environments.
source: Hence, intact CO2 perception allows WCR larvae to locate suitable host plants at agriculturally relevant distances, which may result in specific insect distribution patterns in heterogeneous environments.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of behavioral experiments showing CO2-dependent preference for well-fertilized plants and performance data showing better growth on well-fertilized plants.

claim: Protein tertiary structure and topology prediction models show that the identified genes code for proteins that contain seven transmembrane domains, which is consistent with the protein topology of gustatory and olfactory receptors.
source: Protein tertiary structure and topology prediction models show that the identified genes code for proteins that contain seven transmembrane domains, which is consistent with the protein topology of gustatory and olfactory receptors (Dahanukar et al., 2005; Hallem et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by protein structure prediction models and established knowledge about receptor protein topology from cited literature.

claim: Knocking down DvvGr2 rendered larvae fully unresponsive to synthetic and plant-associated CO2 without impairing responses to other stimuli or affecting search behaviour and motility.
source: Knocking down DvvGr2 rendered larvae fully unresponsive to synthetic and plant-associated CO2 without impairing responses to other stimuli or affecting search behaviour and motility.
evidence: Supported by multiple behavioral experiments showing loss of CO2 response but retention of other sensory responses and normal motility in DvvGr2-silenced larvae.

claim: In Aedes aegypti, Helicoverpa armigera, and Drosophila melanogaster, both carbon dioxide receptors Gr1 and Gr3 are required for CO2 detection.
source: In Aedes aegypti, Helicoverpa armigera, and Drosophila melanogaster, both carbon dioxide receptors Gr1 and Gr3 are required for CO2 detection (Erdelyan et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2007; Kwon et al., 2007; McMeniman et al., 2014; Ning et al., 2016; Suh et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on CO2 receptors in other insect species.

claim: In Culex quinquefasciatus, both Gr2 and Gr3 carbon dioxide receptors are required, while Gr1 acts as a modulator.
source: In Culex quinquefasciatus, both Gr2 and Gr3 carbon dioxide receptors are required, while Gr1 acts as a modulator (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on CO2 receptors in Culex quinquefasciatus.

claim: In Aedes aegypti, the involvement of Gr2 in carbon dioxide responsiveness is still under debate.
source: In A. aegypti, the involvement of Gr2 in carbon dioxide responsiveness is still under debate (Erdelyan et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies with conflicting findings on Gr2 in Aedes aegypti.

claim: The molecular elements required for carbon dioxide perception may be species-specific.
source: Taken together, the molecular elements required for carbon dioxide perception may be species-specific.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of CO2 receptor requirements across different insect species.

claim: DvvGr2, but not DvvGr1 and DvvGr3, are crucial for CO2 responsiveness in WCR.
source: Our results support this notion as DvvGr2, but not DvvGr1 and DvvGr3, are crucial for CO2 responsiveness.
evidence: Supported by gene silencing and behavioral experiments showing that only DvvGr2 silencing eliminates CO2 responsiveness.

claim: The role of DvvGr1 and DvvGr3 for WCR remains to be determined, but their presence and expression may hint at additional complexity in developmental and/or tissue-specific patterns of CO2 responsiveness in this species.
source: The role of DvvGr1 and DvvGr3 for WCR remains to be determined, but their presence and expression may hint at additional complexity in developmental and/or tissue-specific patterns of CO2 responsiveness in this species.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the presence and expression of DvvGr1 and DvvGr3 despite their lack of apparent role in CO2 responsiveness in the tested conditions.

claim: (E)-β-caryophyllene, which is emitted from the roots of certain maize genotypes when they are attacked by root herbivores, attracts second and third instar WCR larvae and allows them to aggregate on maize plants and thereby enhance their fitness.
source: Earlier studies found that (E)-β-caryophyllene, which is emitted from the roots of certain maize genotypes when they are attacked by root herbivores, attracts second and third instar WCR larvae and allows them to aggregate on maize plants and thereby enhance their fitness (Robert et al., 2012b), while neonate larvae are not attracted to this volatile (Hiltpold and Hibbard, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on (E)-β-caryophyllene attraction of WCR larvae.

claim: Ethylene has been shown to attract WCR larvae.
source: Ethylene has also been shown to attract WCR larvae (Robert et al., 2012a), and MBOA or its breakdown products have also been proposed as volatile attractants (Bjostad and Hibbard, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on ethylene attraction of WCR larvae.

claim: MBOA or its breakdown products have been proposed as volatile attractants for WCR larvae.
source: Ethylene has also been shown to attract WCR larvae (Robert et al., 2012a), and MBOA or its breakdown products have also been proposed as volatile attractants (Bjostad and Hibbard, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study proposing MBOA as a volatile attractant.

claim: Methyl anthranilate has been shown to repel WCR larvae.
source: Methyl anthranilate, on the other hand, has been shown to repel WCR larvae (Bernklau et al., 2016b; Bernklau et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on methyl anthranilate repellency to WCR larvae.

claim: Many other leaf- and root-feeding herbivores are known to respond to plant volatiles other than CO2.
source: Many other leaf- and root-feeding herbivores are known to respond to plant volatiles other than CO2 (Bruce et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review on plant volatiles and herbivore responses.

claim: Integrating other volatile cues likely allows WCR larvae to locate maize plants even in the absence of reliable CO2 gradients in the soil, thus increasing the robustness of its foraging behaviour at short distances.
source: Integrating other volatile cues likely allows WCR larvae to locate maize plants even in the absence of reliable CO2 gradients in the soil, thus increasing the robustness of its foraging behaviour at short distances.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that WCR larvae can locate plants at short distances even when CO2 is removed or when CO2 perception is impaired.

claim: WCR larvae show the same efficiency in locating maize roots at short distances in the absence of a CO2 gradient, suggesting that CO2 may not play a role as a cue at close range.
source: An intriguing result in this context is the fact that WCR larvae show the same efficiency in locating maize roots at short distances in the absence of a CO2 gradient, suggesting that this volatile may not play a role as a cue at close range.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral experiments showing similar host location efficiency at short distances with and without CO2 gradients.

claim: A gradient of plant-associated CO2 was detected at distances of up to 32 cm from the plant.
source: A gradient of plant-associated CO2 was detected at distances of up to 32 cm from the plant.
evidence: Supported by CO2 measurements at different distances from plants in soil arenas.

claim: When WCR larvae were released at distances greater than 32 cm, they still managed to locate plants in a DvvGr2-dependent manner.
source: When WCR larvae were released at distances greater than 32 cm, they still managed to locate plants in a DvvGr2-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments in soil arenas showing DvvGr2-dependent host location at distances greater than 32 cm.

claim: The result that WCR larvae locate plants from distances greater than 32 cm can be explained by random movement, where the larvae move randomly until they encounter a CO2 gradient, or by localized CO2 gradients along preferential gas-phase pathways that may extend beyond 32 cm, or a combination of both.
source: This result can be explained by random movement, where the larvae move randomly until they encounter a CO2 gradient, or by localized CO2 gradients along preferential gas-phase pathways that may extend beyond 32 cm, or a combination of both.
evidence: Speculative reasoning to explain how larvae locate plants from distances beyond the measured CO2 gradient.

claim: The advantages of CO2 as a host location cue are that it is abundantly produced through respiration by most organisms, is relatively stable, and diffuses rapidly in air, water, and soil.
source: The advantages of CO2 as a host location cue are that it is abundantly produced through respiration by most organisms, is relatively stable (Jones and Coaker, 1977; Li et al., 2016), and diffuses rapidly in air, water, and soil (Hashimoto and Suzuki, 2002; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about CO2 properties and citations to previous studies.

claim: CO2 may be a suitable long-range cue to locate organisms with high respiratory rates, such as mammals and heterotroph plant parts, including roots and their associated microbial communities.
source: CO2 may thus be a suitable long-range cue to locate organisms with high respiratory rates, such as mammals and heterotroph plant parts, including roots and their associated microbial communities (Johnson and Nielsen, 2012).
evidence: Inferred from the properties of CO2 and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Aboveground insects can be attracted to CO2 traps located as far away as 10 m, and it is estimated that this distance could even be as long as 60 m under optimal environmental circumstances.
source: Aboveground insects can be attracted to CO2 traps located as far away as 10 m, and it is estimated that this distance could even be as long as 60 m under optimal environmental circumstances (Guerenstein and Hildebrand, 2008; Zollner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on CO2 attraction distances for aboveground insects.

claim: For belowground insects, the distance at which CO2 can be detected is hypothesized to be within the lower centimetre range as CO2 diffusion is substantially decreased within the soil matrix compared to CO2 diffusion in air.
source: For belowground insects, this distance is hypothesized to be within the lower centimetre range as CO2 diffusion is substantially decreased within the soil matrix compared to CO2 diffusion in air (Bernklau et al., 2005; Doane et al., 1975; Doane and Klingler, 1978; Klingler, 1966).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on CO2 diffusion in soil and hypothesized detection distances for belowground insects.

claim: Other volatiles that are less abundant and diffuse even less well through the soil such as (E)-β-caryophyllene are unlikely to be detectable at distances of more than 10 cm.
source: Other volatiles that are less abundant and diffuse even less well through the soil such as (E)-β-caryophyllene are unlikely to be detectable at distances of more than 10 cm (Chiriboga M. et al., 2017; Hiltpold and Turlings, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on volatile diffusion in soil.

claim: Volatiles like (E)-β-caryophyllene are likely useful host location cues at short, but not long, distances in the soil.
source: These volatiles are thus likely useful host location cues at short, but not long, distances in the soil.
evidence: Inferred from the limited diffusion distances of volatiles like (E)-β-caryophyllene in soil.

claim: The finding that WCR integrates CO2 perception with other environmental cues and that attraction to CO2 is context dependent is in line with patterns reported for other insects such as mosquitoes and pollinating hawkmoths.
source: The finding that WCR integrates CO2 perception with other environmental cues and that attraction to CO2 is context dependent is in line with patterns reported for other insects such as mosquitoes, whose response to stimuli such as colour, temperature, and human body odours is enhanced by CO2 (McMeniman et al., 2014; van Breugel et al., 2015), and pollinating hawkmoths, which use CO2 as a redundant volatile distance stimulus in a sex-specific manner (Goyret et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by comparison with cited studies on CO2 integration in other insect species.

claim: A CO2 receptor in Drosophila flies is involved in the detection and behavioural responses to other volatiles.
source: A recent study shows that a CO2 receptor in Drosophila flies is also involved in the detection and behavioural responses to other volatiles (MacWilliam et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on CO2 receptor function in Drosophila.

claim: In Drosophila flies, the CO2 receptor Gr63a is required for spermidine attractiveness over short time spans (less than 1 min), but not over longer time spans (hours), when other receptors likely become more important.
source: In Drosophila flies, the CO2 receptor Gr63a is required for spermidine attractiveness over short time spans, that is, less than 1 min, but not over longer time spans (hours), when other receptors likely become more important (MacWilliam et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on CO2 receptor function in Drosophila.

claim: The CO2 scrubber experiment provides evidence that the foraging patterns observed in this study are not due to different sensitivity of DvvGr2-silenced larvae to other root volatiles.
source: The CO2 scrubber experiment provides further evidence that the foraging patterns observed in this study are not due to different sensitivity of DvvGr2-silenced larvae to other root volatiles.
evidence: Inferred from the CO2 scrubber experiments showing that removing CO2 affects both wild type and DvvGr2-silenced larvae similarly, while other volatiles remain unchanged.

claim: CO2 links plant fertilization to herbivore behaviour by guiding WCR to well-fertilized plants.
source: Apart from acting as a long-distance host location cue, CO2 also links plant fertilization to herbivore behaviour by guiding WCR to well-fertilized plants.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments showing CO2-dependent preference for well-fertilized plants.

claim: WCR larvae are resistant to root defences of maize.
source: As WCR larvae are resistant to root defences of maize (Robert et al., 2012b), it is likely to benefit from increased fertilization, independently of the plant's defensive status.
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on WCR resistance to maize defenses.

claim: Following the highest concentrations of CO2 in the soil may be adaptive for the herbivore as it may increase its chance not only to find a maize plant per se but also to identify a plant that has the resources to grow vigorously and that is a better host.
source: As the plant nutritional status and host quality for WCR larvae are associated with higher CO2 release from the roots, following the highest concentrations of CO2 in the soil may be adaptive for the herbivore as it may increase its chance not only to find a maize plant per se but also to identify a plant that has the resources to grow vigorously and that is a better host.
evidence: Inferred from the association between plant fertilization, CO2 release, and larval performance.

claim: Well-fertilized maize plants increase photosynthesis and biomass production, which results in higher CO2 release from the roots.
source: Well-fertilized maize plants increase photosynthesis and biomass production, which results in higher CO2 release from the roots (Zhu and Lynch, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on plant fertilization and CO2 release.

claim: WCR larvae are specialized maize pests that have evolved with intense maize cultivation in the corn belt of the US.
source: WCR larvae are specialized maize pests that have evolved with intense maize cultivation in the corn belt of the US (Gray et al., 2009) and are resistant to maize defence metabolites (Robert et al., 2012b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on WCR evolution and host specialization.

claim: Following the strongest CO2 gradient in an equally spaced maize monoculture may be a useful strategy for WCR to locate suitable food sources.
source: Following the strongest CO2 gradient in an equally spaced maize monoculture may indeed be a useful strategy for this root feeder to locate suitable food sources.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of WCR specialization on maize, resistance to maize defenses, and CO2-dependent preference for well-fertilized plants.

claim: An association between CO2 emission and food-source profitability was suggested for Datura flowers, which emit the highest level of CO2 in times when nectar is most abundant.
source: An association between CO2 emission and food-source profitability was also suggested for Datura flowers, which emit the highest level of CO2 in times when nectar is most abundant (Guerenstein et al., 2004; Thom et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on CO2 emission and nectar availability in Datura flowers.

claim: CO2 is a marker of metabolic activity that allows for an assessment of the vigour and profitability of a wide variety of hosts.
source: These findings support the general hypothesis that CO2 is a marker of metabolic activity that allows for an assessment of the vigour and profitability of a wide variety of hosts.
evidence: Inferred from the findings in this study and comparison with other systems where CO2 is associated with host quality.

claim: The impact of CO2 for the distribution of root herbivores such as the WCR in heterogeneous environments remains to be determined.
source: The impact of CO2 for the distribution of root herbivores such as the WCR in heterogeneous environments remains to be determined.
evidence: Acknowledgment of knowledge gap regarding the ecological implications of CO2-mediated host location.

claim: Based on the results, plant-associated CO2 is expected to contribute to uneven herbivore distribution and to aggregation on plants with a good nutritional status within monocultures.
source: Based on our results, we expect plant-associated CO2 to contribute to uneven herbivore distribution and to aggregation on plants with a good nutritional status within monocultures.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on the experimental findings of CO2-dependent preference for well-fertilized plants.

claim: This work demonstrates how a herbivore uses its capacity to perceive CO2 to locate host plants.
source: In summary, this work demonstrates how a herbivore uses its capacity to perceive CO2 to locate host plants.
evidence: Summary statement supported by the entire body of experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Volatiles other than CO2 are integrated into host-finding behaviour in the soil, but their effects are more important at short than at long distances.
source: Volatiles other than CO2 are also integrated into host-finding behaviour in the soil, but their effects are more important at short than at long distances.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments showing distance-dependent effects of CO2 removal and DvvGr2 silencing on host location.

claim: Random movement in the soil may help WCR to increase its capacity to find host cues at even greater distances.
source: Random movement in the soil may help this root herbivore to increase its capacity to find host cues at even greater distances.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that larvae can locate plants from distances beyond the measured CO2 gradient.

claim: Evidence is accumulating that CO2 acts as an important host location cue in different insects, likely because of its unique role as a highly conserved long-range marker of metabolic activity within complex sensory landscapes.
source: Thus, evidence is now accumulating that CO2 acts as an important host location cue in different insects, likely because of its unique role as a highly conserved long-range marker of metabolic activity within complex sensory landscapes.
evidence: Inferred from the findings in this study and comparison with other systems where CO2 serves as a host location cue.

claim: Datura wrightii flowers emit the highest levels of CO2 during times of high nectar availability.
source: Datura wrightii flowers, for instance, emit the highest levels of CO2 during times of high nectar availability; as hawkmoth pollinators are attracted to CO2, they may thus use this cue to locate rewarding flowers (Goyret et al., 2008; Guerenstein et al., 2004; Guerenstein and Hildebrand, 2008; Stange, 1996; Stange, 1999; Stange and Stowe, 1999; Thom et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on CO2 emission from Datura flowers and hawkmoth attraction.

claim: Hawkmoth pollinators are attracted to CO2 and may use this cue to locate rewarding Datura flowers.
source: Datura wrightii flowers, for instance, emit the highest levels of CO2 during times of high nectar availability; as hawkmoth pollinators are attracted to CO2, they may thus use this cue to locate rewarding flowers (Goyret et al., 2008; Guerenstein et al., 2004; Guerenstein and Hildebrand, 2008; Stange, 1996; Stange, 1999; Stange and Stowe, 1999; Thom et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on hawkmoth attraction to CO2.

claim: Lesions in apples result in high CO2 release and attract Bactrocera tryoni fruit flies.
source: Similarly, lesions in apples result in high CO2 release and attract Bactrocera tryoni fruit flies. As CO2 at corresponding concentrations is attractive to the flies, it has been suggested that they may use plant-associated CO2 to locate suitable oviposition sites (Stange, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study on CO2 release from apple lesions and fruit fly attraction.

claim: Bactrocera tryoni fruit flies may use plant-associated CO2 to locate suitable oviposition sites.
source: Similarly, lesions in apples result in high CO2 release and attract Bactrocera tryoni fruit flies. As CO2 at corresponding concentrations is attractive to the flies, it has been suggested that they may use plant-associated CO2 to locate suitable oviposition sites (Stange, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study suggesting CO2 as an oviposition site location cue.

claim: Root-feeding insects are highly attracted to CO2 in vitro.
source: Root-feeding insects are highly attracted to CO2 in vitro (Bernklau and Bjostad, 1998a; Bernklau and Bjostad, 1998b; Eilers et al., 2012; Hibbard and Bjostad, 1988; Jones and Coaker, 1978; Klingler, 1966; Nicolas and Sillans, 1989; Rogers et al., 2013; Strnad et al., 1986; Strnad and Dunn, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies on CO2 attraction of root-feeding insects.

claim: A likely explanation for the attraction of root-feeding insects to CO2 is that root herbivores use CO2 as a host location cue.
source: Given that CO2 is produced and released by plant roots and diffuses relatively well through the soil, a likely explanation for this phenomenon is that root herbivores use CO2 as a host location cue (Bernklau and Bjostad, 1998a; Bernklau and Bjostad, 1998b; Doane et al., 1975; Erb et al., 2013; Johnson and Gregory, 2006; Johnson and Nielsen, 2012)
evidence: Inferred from the properties of CO2 and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The reliability of CO2 as a host location cue for root feeders has been questioned because CO2 can be emitted by many other sources apart from host plant roots, there is strong diurnal fluctuation in plant CO2 emissions, and other plant-released chemicals can be used by root herbivores for host location within a CO2 background.
source: However, the reliability of CO2 as a host location cue for root feeders has been questioned due to a number of reasons: (i) CO2 can be emitted by many other sources apart from host plant roots, including decaying organic matter, microorganisms, and non-host plants; (ii) there is a strong diurnal fluctuation in plant CO2 emissions that does not necessarily match with insect foraging habits; and (iii) other plant-released chemicals can be used by root herbivores for host location within a CO2 background (Agus et al., 2010; Eilers et al., 2012; Erb et al., 2013; Hansen, 1977; Hibbard and Bjostad, 1988; Hiltpold and Turlings, 2012; Johnson and Nielsen, 2012; Reinecke et al., 2008; Weissteiner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies questioning the reliability of CO2 as a host location cue.

claim: A model that may reconcile different views on CO2 as a host location cue is that CO2 may be used as an initial cue at long distances, while other, more host-specific volatiles may be used at shorter distances.
source: A model that may reconcile these different views is that CO2 may be used as an initial cue at long distances, while other, more host-specific volatiles may be used at shorter distances (Erb et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2006; Johnson and Nielsen, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies proposing a distance-dependent model for CO2 use.

claim: The model that CO2 is used at long distances while other volatiles are used at short distances has not been experimentally validated prior to this study.
source: So far, this model has not been experimentally validated, and the precise role of plant-associated CO2 as a host location cue by herbivores, in general, and root herbivores, in particular, remains unclear (Eilers et al., 2016).
evidence: Acknowledgment of knowledge gap and citation to a previous review.

claim: No studies prior to this one have investigated the role of plant-associated CO2 in plant–herbivore interactions in vivo using molecular manipulative approaches.
source: To the best of our knowledge, no studies so far have investigated the role of plant-associated CO2 in plant–herbivore interactions in vivo using molecular manipulative approaches.
evidence: Statement of novelty based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The larvae of Diabrotica virgifera virgifera (WCR) feed almost exclusively on maize roots in agricultural settings and cause major yield losses in the US and Eastern Europe.
source: The larvae of Diabrotica virgifera virgifera (the western corn rootworm [WCR]) feed almost exclusively on maize roots in agricultural settings and cause major yield losses in the US and Eastern Europe (Ciosi et al., 2008; Gray et al., 2009; Meinke et al., 2009; Toepfer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on WCR biology and economic impact.

claim: WCR larvae rely on a number of volatile and non-volatile chemicals to identify and locate host plants, and distinguish between suitable and less-suitable maize plants and forage within the maize root system.
source: The larvae rely on a number of volatile and non-volatile chemicals to identify and locate host plants, and distinguish between suitable and less-suitable maize plants and forage within the maize root system (Hiltpold et al., 2013; Johnson and Gregory, 2006; Johnson and Nielsen, 2012; Robert et al., 2012c; Schumann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on WCR chemical ecology.

claim: Non-volatile primary metabolites such as sugars and fatty acids as well as secondary metabolites such as benzoxazinoids and phenolic acid conjugates modulate WCR larval behaviour.
source: Non-volatile primary metabolites such as sugars and fatty acids as well as secondary metabolites such as benzoxazinoids and phenolic acid conjugates modulate larval behaviour (Bernklau et al., 2011; Bernklau et al., 2015; Bernklau et al., 2016a; Bernklau et al., 2018; Erb et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2017; Machado et al., 2021; Robert et al., 2012c).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on non-volatile compounds affecting WCR behavior.

claim: Volatiles including (E)-β-caryophyllene, ethylene, and CO2 attract WCR larvae.
source: Volatiles including (E)-β-caryophyllene, ethylene, and CO2 attract the larvae (Bernklau and Bjostad, 1998a; Bernklau and Bjostad, 1998b; Robert et al., 2012b; Robert et al., 2012a)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on volatile attractants for WCR larvae.

claim: Based on the finding that high CO2 levels can outweigh the attractive effects of other maize volatiles, it was suggested that CO2 may be the only relevant volatile attractant for WCR larvae.
source: Based on the finding that high CO2 levels can outweigh the attractive effects of other maize volatiles, it was suggested that CO2 may be the only relevant volatile attractant for WCR larvae (Bernklau and Bjostad, 1998b).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study suggesting CO2 as the primary attractant.

claim: Under conditions where CO2 levels are similar, WCR larvae reliably choose between host plants of different suitability using other volatile cues.
source: However, under conditions where CO2 levels are similar, WCR larvae reliably choose between host plants of different suitability using other volatile cues (Huang et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2016; Robert et al., 2012b; Robert et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies showing WCR responses to volatiles other than CO2.

claim: Putative CO2 receptors have been identified from WCR transcriptomic data.
source: The demonstrated ability of WCR larvae to respond to different volatile cues and the recent identification of putative CO2 receptors from transcriptomic data (Rodrigues et al., 2016) make this species a suitable model system to investigate the role of CO2 in plant–herbivore interactions.
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous transcriptomic study.

claim: Ongoing efforts exist to use CO2 as a bait to control WCR in the field.
source: Ongoing efforts to use CO2 as a bait to control WCR in the field (Bernklau et al., 2004; Schumann et al., 2014a; Schumann et al., 2014b) provide further motivation to assess the importance of this volatile for WCR foraging.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on CO2-based WCR control strategies.

claim: Silencing CO2 perception or scrubbing plant-associated CO2 has no effect on the ability of WCR larvae to locate host plants at short distances (<9 cm), but impairs host location at greater distances.
source: Silencing CO2 perception or scrubbing plant-associated CO2 has no effect on the ability of WCR larvae to locate host plants at short distances (<9 cm), but impairs host location at greater distances.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments showing distance-dependent effects of CO2 removal and DvvGr2 silencing on host location.

claim: WCR larvae preferentially orient and prefer plants that grow in well-fertilized soils compared to plants that grow in nutrient-poor soils, a behaviour that has direct consequences for larval growth and depends on the ability of the larvae to perceive root-emitted CO2.
source: WCR larvae preferentially orient and prefer plants that grow in well-fertilized soils compared to plants that grow in nutrient-poor soils, a behaviour that has direct consequences for larval growth and depends on the ability of the larvae to perceive root-emitted CO2.
evidence: Supported by behavioral choice experiments and performance assays with differentially fertilized plants.

claim: The expression of a carbon dioxide receptor, DvvGr2, is specifically required for dose-dependent larval responses to CO2.
source: The expression of a carbon dioxide receptor, DvvGr2, is specifically required for dose-dependent larval responses to CO2.
evidence: Supported by gene silencing experiments and dose-response behavioral assays.
